one_liner: CLI data-wrangling toolkit that computes CSV summary stats far faster than pandas describe, no DataFrame required.
what_it_does: qsv is a single Rust binary with roughly 50 subcommands (stats, frequency, join, sqlp, schema, geocode, etc.) for wrangling CSV, Excel, and other tabular files, used as a CLI rather than imported as a library. Its `stats` subcommand infers a guaranteed data type per column (Null/String/Float/Integer/Date/DateTime/Boolean) and computes up to 48 summary statistics, covering the same ground as pandas' `.describe()`. Because it's a shell tool, integrating it means shelling out or piping, not calling a Python API.
how_it_is_fast: `stats` streams the file once and computes its default statistic set (sum, min/max, mean, stddev, sparsity, etc.) in constant memory instead of materializing a DataFrame, and it multithreads per-column work once a `qsv index` (.idx) exists for the file. The non-streaming statistics that need the whole dataset (median, quartiles, mode, cardinality) use a memory-aware chunking algorithm rather than a naive full load. `stats` also assumes the CSV is well-formed and UTF-8, letting it skip repeated UTF-8 validation and bounds checks that a general-purpose parser like pandas' would perform.
when_to_use: One-off or scripted CSV summary stats / type inference from shell pipelines, Makefiles, or CI, without spinning up Python or pandas.
You can build a `qsv index` for the file first (or set QSV_AUTOINDEX_SIZE) to unlock multithreaded stats, frequency, split, and instant count/slice/sample.
You need guaranteed, deterministic type inference per column rather than pandas' best-effort dtype guessing.
Large CSVs (hundreds of MB to tens of GB) where you want the default 'streaming' stats in constant memory rather than a full in-memory DataFrame.
Batch/ETL contexts where a standalone compiled CLI (or its MCP server) is an acceptable dependency.
when_not_to_use: You need the result as an in-memory DataFrame/array for further Python computation — qsv emits CSV/JSON text, not a DataFrame object.
Your CSVs are malformed or non-UTF-8: `stats` explicitly assumes well-formed, valid UTF-8 input and warns of undefined behavior otherwise; run `qsv validate` first.
You need the full 48-statistic 'advanced' set (median, quartiles, mode, cardinality) on very large files without accepting an extra chunked, higher-memory pass.
Team is Python-only and can't add a separate compiled binary/CLI step to the pipeline.

You want a reproducible, modern-hardware performance claim: the 75x/6x numbers are from an April 2022 maintainer GitHub Discussion post, not a benchmark suite, with no hardware or compiler flags given for that specific run.

integration.dependencies: none for prebuilt binaries; building from source pulls in many optional, feature-gated crates (Polars, DuckDB-backed commands, Luau, geocoding databases, etc.) — the project's Cargo.toml notes `cargo install qsv` from crates.io is not currently supported
integration.min_toolchain: Rust 1.98 (edition 2024), per Cargo.toml and the README badge
integration.platforms: Linux (x86_64 GNU/musl, aarch64 GNU), macOS (Apple Silicon), Windows (x86_64 MSVC, aarch64), plus IBM Power (PowerPC64 LE) and IBM Z (s390x); prebuilt x86_64 binaries deliberately skip CPU-specific optimizations to avoid SIGILL faults across CPU variants
integration.thread_safety: not documented as a library API (qsv is a CLI process, not embeddable); internally, `stats`/`frequency`/`split`/`schema`/`tojsonl` multithread per-column/per-chunk work once an index is built
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — explain: same problem (CSV summary statistics + type inference) as pandas describe, but a different interface entirely: a CLI subcommand you shell out to or pipe through, not a Python API returning a DataFrame

gotchas: `stats` assumes a well-formed, UTF-8 CSV and skips validation for speed; malformed input is explicitly undefined behavior — run `qsv validate` first if unsure.
Multithreading, instant `count`/`slice`/`sample`, and faster `stats`/`frequency`/`schema`/`split` only kick in once you build a `qsv index`; without one, stats runs single-threaded and streaming.

Only the default 'streaming' statistics run in constant memory; median, quartiles, mode/antimode, and cardinality require loading more data (via a memory-aware chunker, not the naive whole file) and must be enabled explicitly (e.g. `--everything`).
GitHub's UI reports the license as NOASSERTION; the repo's own LICENSE-MIT, COPYING, and Cargo.toml confirm MIT-only licensing since v21.1.1 (dual MIT/Unlicense in v21.1.1 and earlier).
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick qsv over xan, zsv, or DuckDB's CSV reader when you want one CLI with dozens of built-in wrangling verbs (join, dedupe, geocode, schema/JSON-Schema inference, Polars-backed SQL) beyond just fast parsing or stats. Pick zsv or xan instead when raw parse/read throughput is the goal — zsv's own darwin-arm64 shootout benchmarks it directly against qsv (and xsv, xan) and shows it ahead on parsing speed.
verified_claims_summary: On a 124MB, 2.7M-row CSV, qsv's default `stats` finished in under 0.16s versus pandas computing comparable stats in 12s (75x faster), and `stats --everything` (48 measures) took 2s (6x faster); these are the maintainer's own numbers from an April 28, 2022 GitHub Discussion post, with no hardware or compiler flags disclosed for that specific comparison (a separate footnote's 22.4s/Ryzen 7 4800H figure is for a different, larger NYC-311 run with no pandas comparison).
status_note: Actively maintained (commits as recently as today) and MIT-licensed since v21.1.1; ships as prebuilt binaries for all major OS/arch combinations or builds from a Rust 1.98 source tree, making it straightforward to vendor as a standalone CLI tool.
